App.Name: Artemis 26
Home.Pitch: Build the spacecraft. Fly a week that really happened. Find out what you should have packed.

Event.Storm.Name: Geomagnetic storm, Kp {kp}
Fact.MissDistance: {km} km from Earth's centre, {lunar} times the Moon's distance
Fact.Diameter: Estimated {min} to {max} m across, from its brightness
Fact.Kp: Strongest reading in this leg: Kp {kp} of 9
Fact.ParticlesYes: Energetic particles detected near Earth in the day before the storm or during it
Fact.ParticlesNo: No energetic particle event detected near Earth in the day before the storm or during it
Fact.FlareObserved: Strongest flare in the three days before the storm or during it: class {flare}
Fact.FlareAssumed: Flare class {flare}, assumed from the storm's strength
Learned.Storm: The Kp index runs from 0 to 9, and 5 or more counts as a geomagnetic storm. The strongest reading in this leg was {kp}.
Fact.FlareNone: No class M or X flare in the three days before the storm or during it
Learned.Asteroid.2019OK: 2019 OK passed 71,355 km from Earth's centre, less than a fifth of the Moon's distance, at 24.5 km/s. Its size is estimated at 58 to 130 m from its brightness.
Fact.Dart.Parent: It orbits Didymos, an asteroid 780 m across
Learned.Rare.DartImpact: On 26 September 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos, a moonlet 160 m across. It was the first mission to test deflecting an asteroid by hitting it.
Fact.Grb.Rate: A burst this bright is expected about once in 10,000 years
Learned.Rare.Grb221009A: On 9 October 2022 a pulse of radiation swept through the solar system. It was likely the brightest gamma-ray burst since human civilization began.
Learned.Exoplanet.TRAPPIST1e: TRAPPIST-1 e is a terrestrial planet a little smaller than Earth. It orbits an M-type star every 6.1 days.
Learned.Exoplanet.51Pegb: 51 Pegasi b is a gas giant that circles its star every 4.2 days. Its discovery was announced in 1995.
Learned.Exoplanet.ProximaCenb: Proxima Centauri b orbits an M-type star every 11.2 days. Its discovery was announced in 2016.
Learned.Exoplanet.WASP39b: In 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope found the first clear evidence of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of a planet outside the solar system. This is that planet.
Image.AsteroidA: Representative image: asteroid Ida and its moon Dactyl, from NASA's Galileo spacecraft
Image.AsteroidB: Representative image: asteroid Gaspra, from NASA's Galileo spacecraft
Image.AsteroidC: Representative image: the saddle of asteroid Eros, from NASA's NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft
Image.Storm: Representative image: aurora from a geomagnetic storm, photographed from the International Space Station in January 2026
Image.StormSevere: Representative image: the X9.3 solar flare of 6 September 2017, from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory
Image.ExoplanetVisible: Representative illustration: the TRAPPIST-1 planets crossing their star
Image.ExoplanetSpectrum: Representative illustration: a hot Jupiter whose clouds hide its water
Image.DartImpact: Illustration: the DART spacecraft approaching Dimorphos and Didymos
Image.Grb221009A: X-ray image of GRB 221009A from NASA's Swift telescope. The rings are X-rays scattered by dust in our own galaxy
Fact.Observed.SeenBeforeAndAfter: NASA/JPL's observations of it run from {first} to {last}
Fact.Observed.LastSeenBefore: Last observation on record: {last}. This pass is computed from its orbit
Learned.Asteroid.SeenBeforeAndAfter: {name} passed {km} km from Earth's centre, {lunar} times the Moon's distance. Its orbit rests on observations from {first} to {last}.
Learned.Asteroid.FirstSeenAfter: {name} passed {km} km from Earth's centre before anyone had recorded it. Its first observation is dated {first}. Surveys keep scanning the sky because of passes like this.
Learned.Asteroid.LastSeenBefore: The last observation of {name} on record is dated {last}. This pass, {km} km from Earth's centre, is computed from its orbit.
Learned.Mode.Transit: {name} dims its star a little each time it crosses in front. The depth of the dip gives the planet's size.
Learned.Mode.RadialVelocity: {name} tugs its star back and forth. The size of the wobble gives a lower limit on the planet's mass.
Learned.Mode.Imaging: {name} was photographed directly. That takes a planet bright enough, and far enough from its star, to be picked out of the glare.
Sources.Note.Planets: Planets are standing targets. The game does not time them to their real transits.
Sources.Note.Estimates: Asteroid sizes are estimates from brightness. Each pass is computed by NASA/JPL from the asteroid's orbit; the card says when it was actually observed.
Week.Title: Choose a week
Week.JulyNineteen.Name: A fifth of the way to the Moon
Week.JulyNineteen.About: A quiet Sun, and asteroid 2019 OK passing closer than most satellites orbit.
Week.AutumnTwentyTwo.Name: Impact and burst
Week.AutumnTwentyTwo.About: NASA's DART spacecraft strikes an asteroid. Two weeks later comes the brightest gamma-ray burst on record.
Week.MayTwentyFour.Name: The great storm
Week.MayTwentyFour.About: The strongest geomagnetic storm in two decades. Shields decide this one.
